title: Odd plus odd is even
plain: The sum of two odd natural numbers is even.
math: For all $a,b\in\mathbb N$, if $a$ and $b$ are odd then $a+b$ is even.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-Q1: Odd plus odd is even
The sum of two odd natural numbers is even.
Informal statement: For all $a,b\in\mathbb N$, if $a$ and $b$ are odd then $a+b$ is even.
Formalization notes: Uses Mathlib's `Odd` and `Even`.
This is a submission-system test problem with a known solution; prove `Claim`.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDQ1
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ a b : ℕ, Odd a → Odd b → Even (a + b)

end OpenProblems.QEDQ1

title: n² + n is even

title: Sum of the first n odd numbers
plain: Adding up the first n odd numbers 1 + 3 + 5 + … gives n².
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-Q3: Sum of the first n odd numbers
Adding up the first n odd numbers 1 + 3 + 5 + … gives n².
Informal statement: For all $n$, $\sum_{i<n}(2i+1)=n^2$.
Formalization notes: Sum over `Finset.range n` in ℕ.
This is a submission-system test problem with a known solution; prove `Claim`.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDQ3
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℕ, ∑ i ∈ Finset.range n, (2 * i + 1) = n ^ 2

end OpenProblems.QEDQ3
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 8 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed.

title: Nicomachus: sum of cubes
plain: The sum of the first n cubes equals the square of the sum of the first n numbers.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-Q4: Nicomachus: sum of cubes
The sum of the first n cubes equals the square of the sum of the first n numbers.
Informal statement: For all $n$, $\sum_{i=0}^{n} i^3=\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n} i\right)^2$.
Formalization notes: Sums over `Finset.range (n + 1)` in ℕ.
This is a submission-system test problem with a known solution; prove `Claim`.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDQ4
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℕ, ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), i ^ 3 = (∑ i ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), i) ^ 2

end OpenProblems.QEDQ4
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 16 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed.

title: Party of six (R(3,3) ≤ 6)
plain: Among any six people, some three all know each other or some three are all strangers.
math: Every simple graph on 6 vertices contains a triangle or an independent set of size 3.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-Q6: Party of six (R(3,3) ≤ 6)
Among any six people, some three all know each other or some three are all strangers.
Informal statement: Every simple graph on 6 vertices contains a triangle or an independent set of size 3.
Formalization notes: `G` ranges over all simple graphs on `Fin 6`; the three vertices must be distinct.
This is a submission-system test problem with a known solution; prove `Claim`.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDQ6
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin 6), ∃ a b c : Fin 6, a ≠ b ∧ b ≠ c ∧ a ≠ c ∧
    ((G.Adj a b ∧ G.Adj b c ∧ G.Adj a c) ∨ (¬ G.Adj a b ∧ ¬ G.Adj b c ∧ ¬ G.Adj a c))

end OpenProblems.QEDQ6
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 64 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed.

title: Erdős–Szekeres monotone subsequences
plain: Any list of rs + 1 distinct real numbers has an increasing run of r + 1 of them or a decreasing run of s + 1 of them (not necessarily consecutive).
math: For $f:\{0,\dots,rs\}\to\mathbb R$ injective there is a set of $r+1$ indices on which $f$ is strictly increasing, or a set of $s+1$ indices on which it is strictly decreasing.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-Q7: Erdős–Szekeres monotone subsequences
Any list of rs + 1 distinct real numbers has an increasing run of r + 1 of them or a decreasing run of s + 1 of them (not necessarily consecutive).
Informal statement: For $f:\{0,\dots,rs\}\to\mathbb R$ injective there is a set of $r+1$ indices on which $f$ is strictly increasing, or a set of $s+1$ indices on which it is strictly decreasing.
Formalization notes: Indices are `Fin (r * s + 1)`; subsequences are finite sets of indices with `StrictMonoOn`/`StrictAntiOn`.
This is a submission-system test problem with a known solution; prove `Claim`.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDQ7
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ (r s : ℕ) (f : Fin (r * s + 1) → ℝ), Function.Injective f →
    (∃ t : Finset (Fin (r * s + 1)), t.card = r + 1 ∧ StrictMonoOn f (t : Set (Fin (r * s + 1)))) ∨
    (∃ t : Finset (Fin (r * s + 1)), t.card = s + 1 ∧ StrictAntiOn f (t : Set (Fin (r * s + 1))))

end OpenProblems.QEDQ7
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 128 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed.

title: Dilworth's theorem
plain: In any finite partially ordered set, the largest number of pairwise incomparable elements equals the smallest number of chains needed to cover everything.
math: For every finite poset $P$ there are $k$, an antichain of size $k$, and a partition of $P$ into $k$ chains.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-Q8: Dilworth's theorem
In any finite partially ordered set, the largest number of pairwise incomparable elements equals the smallest number of chains needed to cover everything.
Informal statement: For every finite poset $P$ there are $k$, an antichain of size $k$, and a partition of $P$ into $k$ chains.
Formalization notes: Stated as: some antichain `A` of size `k` and a colouring `c : α → Fin k` whose colour classes are chains. (Any antichain meets each chain at most once, so this is exactly Dilworth.)
This is a submission-system test problem with a known solution; prove `Claim`.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDQ8
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ (α : Type) [Fintype α] [PartialOrder α], ∃ (k : ℕ) (A : Finset α) (c : α → Fin k),
    IsAntichain (· ≤ ·) (A : Set α) ∧ A.card = k ∧ ∀ x y : α, c x = c y → (x ≤ y ∨ y ≤ x)

end OpenProblems.QEDQ8
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 256 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed.
